isSafe.question: Is endoscopy a safe procedure?
isSafe.answer: Yes, endoscopy is one of the safest medical procedures when performed by a specialized doctor with modern equipment, with a very low complication rate.

sedation.question: Is endoscopy painful, and will I be conscious during it?
sedation.answer: The procedure is usually done under light sedation (conscious sedation), so you won't feel pain or discomfort, and you'll wake up within minutes of it ending.

pain.question: Will I feel pain after the procedure?
pain.answer: You may feel mild bloating or a slight sore throat for a few hours, which is normal and resolves quickly without needing strong painkillers.

recoveryTime.question: How many days will I need to fully recover?
recoveryTime.answer: You can usually return to your daily activities the same day or the next, and we only recommend avoiding driving for 24 hours after sedation.

afterEffects.question: Are there any side effects after the endoscopy?
afterEffects.answer: Some patients feel mild bloating or a slight change in their voice for a short while — temporary effects that disappear within hours.

cost.question: Does the consultation and endoscopy cost include everything?
cost.answer: The cost is explained in full detail from the first consultation, covering the procedure, sedation, and follow-up, with no additional surprises.

howToBook.question: How can I book an appointment?
howToBook.answer: You can easily book your appointment by calling directly or reaching out on WhatsApp, and our team will help you choose the nearest suitable time.

completeGuide.title: The Complete Guide to Digestive Health: Warning Signs and Prevention Steps
completeGuide.excerpt: Everything you need to know about maintaining digestive health, from early warning signs to the daily prevention habits recommended by the latest medical research.
completeGuide.content:
Digestive health is the foundation of your overall wellbeing, yet many of us ignore the early warning signs our body sends before they become a chronic problem.

Key signs to watch for include persistent bloating after eating, a sudden change in bowel habits, feeling full too quickly, or recurring pain in the upper abdomen. If any of these persist for more than two weeks, it's time to see a specialist.

On the prevention side, modern medical research emphasizes the importance of dietary fiber, adequate hydration, and cutting back on processed foods and saturated fats. Even simple daily movement, like a 30-minute walk, noticeably improves bowel function.

Regular screening matters, especially if you have a family history of digestive diseases or are over 40. Early diagnosis makes a huge difference in how easy treatment is and how likely a full recovery becomes.

refluxVsHeartburn.title: The Difference Between Regular Heartburn and Chronic Acid Reflux
refluxVsHeartburn.excerpt: Not every heartburn after eating means acid reflux. Learn the differences and the signs that need medical follow-up.
refluxVsHeartburn.content:
Many people use "heartburn" and "reflux" interchangeably, but there's an important difference worth understanding.

Ordinary heartburn usually follows a heavy or spicy meal and fades on its own within an hour or two. Chronic acid reflux (GERD), on the other hand, is an ongoing condition where stomach acid repeatedly flows back into the esophagus, causing symptoms like chest burning, difficulty swallowing, and sometimes a chronic cough or hoarse voice.

The key distinction is frequency: chronic reflux happens more than twice a week and affects your daily quality of life. If your symptoms keep recurring, a simple gastroscopy can pinpoint the real cause and guide the right treatment.

ibsCauses.title: IBS: The Real Causes and Modern Treatment Methods
ibsCauses.excerpt: A comprehensive look at the causes of irritable bowel syndrome and the latest treatment protocols that improve daily quality of life.
ibsCauses.content:
IBS is one of the most frustrating conditions for patients, since its symptoms often come and go without an obvious trigger.

The real causes behind IBS are varied: stress and anxiety, sensitivity to certain foods, an imbalance in healthy gut bacteria, or heightened sensitivity of the intestines to normal post-meal stretching.

Modern treatment now takes an integrated approach: dietary adjustments (like a low-FODMAP diet), stress management through relaxation techniques, and sometimes probiotics to support gut health. Treatment is tailored to each case, since the underlying causes differ from person to person.

fattyLiverGuide.title: Everything You Need to Know About Fatty Liver Before It Progresses
fattyLiverGuide.excerpt: A simple guide to understanding what causes fat buildup in the liver, and when a mild case turns into a real concern.
fattyLiverGuide.content:
Fatty liver has become one of the most common conditions today, driven largely by unhealthy lifestyles and obesity.

There are two main types: simple fatty liver, which often has no clear symptoms and causes little harm if treated early, and inflammatory fatty liver (NASH), which can progress to liver fibrosis if ignored.

Signs to watch for include persistent fatigue, mild pain in the upper right abdomen, and sometimes abnormal liver test results during a routine checkup.

The good news is that simple fatty liver often improves with dietary changes, gradual weight loss, and regular exercise. Regular follow-up with a liver specialist is important to prevent the condition from progressing.

endoscopyPrep.title: Proper Preparation Steps for Gastroscopy and Colonoscopy
endoscopyPrep.excerpt: Practical guidance that ensures a safe, comfortable procedure, from fasting to the day of the procedure itself.
endoscopyPrep.content:
Proper preparation for an endoscopy ensures a safe procedure and accurate results, while minimizing the risk of complications.

For 6–8 hours before the procedure, you should fast completely, with only small sips of water allowed up to two hours beforehand. If you take blood thinners, tell your doctor in advance so they can advise on stopping or adjusting the dose.

On the day of the procedure, it's best to bring someone who can drive you home afterward, especially if light sedation will be used. Wear comfortable clothing and leave jewelry or metal items at home.

Right after the procedure, you'll need a short rest period until the sedation wears off, after which you can gently return to your normal activities.

postEndoscopyNutrition.title: Proper Nutrition After Endoscopic Procedures
postEndoscopyNutrition.excerpt: A gradual diet plan that helps you recover quickly and safely after any endoscopic procedure.
postEndoscopyNutrition.content:
Proper nutrition after any endoscopic procedure plays a big role in how quickly you recover and how comfortable you feel.

For the first couple of hours afterward, stick to clear liquids like water and light tea. After that, gradually move to soft foods like soup, yogurt, and bananas, avoiding spicy or fatty foods for at least a day.

If a biopsy was taken during the procedure, your doctor may recommend a specific diet until results come back. Most importantly, listen to your body — if you notice anything unusual like severe pain or bleeding, contact the clinic immediately.

liverFunctionTests.title: When Is a Liver Function Test Necessary?
liverFunctionTests.excerpt: The signs and conditions that call for an immediate liver function test, and how to correctly read the results.
liverFunctionTests.content:
A liver function test is a simple diagnostic tool that reveals a great deal about your overall liver health.

Situations that call for an immediate test include unexplained fatigue lasting a long time, yellowing of the skin or eyes, pain in the upper right abdomen, or having risk factors like obesity or a family history of liver disease.

Results typically include markers like ALT and AST enzymes and bilirubin levels. A slight elevation can be temporary and harmless, but a sustained or significant rise needs careful evaluation by a specialist to determine the real cause and appropriate treatment.
